# Brief: class notes, Sistemas de Comunicação (CamScanner scan, 17 pages)

The notes are handwritten in Portuguese and were read visually at 100 DPI. The text layer is empty. A few small details are hard to read, and I flag them below. The notes cover four topics:
- Binary symmetric channel (BSC) and probability review.
- Repetition code.
- Information theory: information and entropy.
- Huffman source coding, ending with an introduction to Hamming codes.

## 1. Binary symmetric channel (BSC) and probability review (pp. 1–2)
- **Setup.**
  - A binary signal (0 or 1) goes from the transmitter (X) to the receiver (Y). Each bit is expected to arrive unchanged (p. 1).
  - The diagram shows 0→0 and 1→1 with probability 1−Pe, and the crossovers 0→1 and 1→0 with probability Pe (p. 1).
  - Pe is the "probability of error" or "crossover probability", and it is a conditional probability. Noise is what flips the bits (p. 1).
  - "Symmetric" means the 0→1 and 1→0 flip probabilities are equal (p. 1).
  - FSK note: a wave is a sequence of 0s and 1s, and each symbol is a specific frequency (p. 1).
- **Joint probability.** P(A,B) = P(A∩B) = P(B)·P(A|B) = P(A)·P(B|A). It does not mean the events happen at the same time (p. 1).
- **Conditional probability and Bayes.** P(B|A) = P(B)·P(A|B) / P(A) (p. 2).
- **Definition of Pe.** Pe = P(Y=0|X=1) = P(Y=1|X=0) (p. 2).
- **Worked example (p. 2).**
  - Given Pe = 0.1, P(X=0) = 0.6, P(X=1) = 0.4.
  - Questions: (a) P(Y=0) and P(Y=1); (b) P(X=0|Y=0), P(X=1|Y=0), P(X=0|Y=1), P(X=1|Y=1).
  - Part (a) is set up as P(Y=0) = P(X=0,Y=0) + P(X=1,Y=0).
  - The notes compute P(X=0,Y=0) = 0.6 · 0.9 = 0.54. Here 0.9 = 1−Pe, the probability of no error.
  - **The notes stop there.** My completion, not in the notes: P(X=1,Y=0) = 0.4·0.1 = 0.04, so P(Y=0) = 0.58 and P(Y=1) = 0.42. Part (b) then follows from Bayes, for example P(X=0|Y=0) = 0.54/0.58 ≈ 0.931.

## 2. Repetition code (pp. 3–6)
- **Idea.** Send 0 as 000…0 and 1 as 111…1 (n bits). The larger n is, the smaller the chance of misinterpretation (p. 3).
- **Single error in 5 bits.** Bit errors are independent. For sent 11111 and received 01111, P = Pe·(1−Pe)⁴. So P(1 error in 5) = 5·Pe·(1−Pe)⁴ (p. 3).
- **Binomial formula.** C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n−k)!), and P(k errors in n bits) = C(n,k)·Peᵏ·(1−Pe)ⁿ⁻ᵏ (pp. 4).
  - Example: P(2 errors in 5 bits) = C(5,2)·Pe²·(1−Pe)³, with C(5,2) = 10 (p. 4).
  - The notes list the received patterns 00111, 01011 and 10011 for sent 11111 (p. 4).
- **RC(1,n).** n is the code order and **must be odd** (p. 4).
  - Example with n = 3 and 0 sent as 000:
    - 000 means no error.
    - 001, 010 and 100 are decoded as 000, assuming Pe is low.
    - 101, 011, 110 and 111 are decoding errors, because simple majority voting picks 1 (p. 4).
- **Decoding error probability.** P_DE = P(majority of bits wrong) = P(at least (n+1)/2 bits wrong) (p. 5).
  - Worked example: Pe = 0.2 and RC(1,3).
    - P(2 errors) = C(3,2)·0.2²·0.8 = 0.096.
    - P(3 errors) = 0.2³ = 0.008.
    - P_DE = 0.104 = **10.4%**, compared with 20% when sending a single bit (p. 5).
- **General formula.** P_DE = Σ from k=(n+1)/2 to n of C(n,k)·Peᵏ·(1−Pe)ⁿ⁻ᵏ (p. 6).

## 3. Information theory (pp. 6–10)
- **Scope.** Information ≠ data. The aim is to measure the quantity of information in a random variable's or experiment's outcomes, and to measure entropy (p. 6).
- **Information of an event A.** I(A) = −log₂ P(A), in bits (p. 6).
  - On p. 6 the minus sign is missing from the handwriting. Page 7 uses −log₂, and the graph −log(x) confirms it.
  - Low probability gives high I(A). High probability gives low I(A). The sketch shows I(A) → ∞ as P(A) → 0, and I(A) = 0 at P(A) = 1 (p. 6).
- **Fair die example.** P(X=k) = 1/6. For A = [X=5], I(A) = −log₂(1/6) = log₂6 ≈ **2.585 bits** (p. 7).
- **Entropy is** (p. 7):
  - the average quantity of information;
  - a measure of "disorder";
  - the difficulty of predicting the outcome;
  - the number of binary (yes/no) questions needed to determine the outcome.
- **Definition.** H(X) = −Σ (k=1..N) P(X=xₖ)·log₂ P(X=xₖ). Units are bits or bits/symbol (p. 7).
- **Examples.**
  - Fair coin: H = −(½·(−1) + ½·(−1)) = **1 bit**, which is one question (p. 8).
  - Fair die: H = log₂6 = **2.585 bits** (p. 8).
  - Loaded die with P(1) = 0.9 and P(k) = 0.02 for k = 2–6: H = −(0.9·log₂0.9 + 5·0.02·log₂0.02) ≈ **0.7 bit** (p. 9).
  - Object in one of 16 positions, each with probability 1/16 (pp. 9–10):
    - I(X≠1) = log₂16 − log₂15.
    - P(X≠2|X≠1) = 14/15, so I = log₂15 − log₂14.
    - P(X≠3|X≠1,2) = 13/14, so I = log₂14 − log₂13.
    - The terms cancel in the sum, leaving log₂16.
    - H = −16·(1/16)·log₂(1/16) = log₂16 = **4 bits**.
- **Observations (p. 9).**
  - Usually, the larger the sample space, the larger the entropy.
  - Maximum entropy occurs for a uniform distribution (equiprobable outcomes).
  - Minimum entropy (zero) occurs when some outcome is certain, P(X=xₖ) = 1.

## 4. Coding and Huffman code (pp. 10–16)
- **Two types of coding (p. 10).**
  - Channel coding is error detection and correction. Example: the repetition code.
  - Source coding is data compression. It is lossless (for example text) or lossy (for example audio, image and video).
- **Huffman code (p. 11).**
  - It is lossless compression that reduces message redundancy.
  - Less probable symbols get longer codewords, and more probable symbols get shorter ones.
  - The lowest possible rate in bits/symbol is the source entropy. Lower entropy allows more compression. A margin note says the uniform distribution gives maximum entropy.
- **Method (pp. 11–12).** The alphabet is A = {a₁…aₙ} with pₖ = P(aₖ) and Σpₖ = 1.
  1. Sort the symbols by probability, from highest to lowest.
  2. Replace the two least probable symbols with a new symbol whose probability is their sum.
  3. Reorder the new list, then repeat steps 2 and 3 until only 2 symbols remain.
  4. This builds a binary tree. Assign 0 and 1 to the branches to define each codeword.
- **Worked example (pp. 12–13).**
  - Probabilities: a₁ = 0.7, a₂ = 0.12, a₃ = 0.1, a₄ = 0.08.
  - Fixed-length code 00, 01, 10, 11 gives L = Σpₖlₖ = 2 bits/symbol (p. 12).
  - Entropy H = −Σpₖlog₂pₖ = **1.351 bit/symbol** (p. 13).
  - Tree merges: a₃+a₄ = 0.18, then 0.18+a₂ = 0.3, then 0.3 against a₁ = 0.7 (p. 13).
  - Huffman code: a₁→0, a₂→11, a₃→100, a₄→101 (p. 13).
  - Average length L = 1(0.7) + 2(0.12) + 3(0.1) + 3(0.08) = **1.48 bit/symbol** (p. 13).
  - Efficiency η = H/L = 1.351/1.48 ≈ 0.9128 (91.28%) (p. 13).
  - Redundancy γ = 1−η ≈ 0.0872 (p. 13).
- **Properties of Huffman code (p. 14).** It is uniquely decodable, prefix-free and instantaneous.
  - Kraft–McMillan inequality: Σ2^(−lₖ) ≤ 1. The notes say it is necessary but not sufficient.
  - Huffman is optimal when P(aₖ) = 1/2ⁿ with n an integer.
  - Example: probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.25 give codes 0, 10, 11 and L = 1.5. Then H = 1.5, η = 1 and γ = 0 (pp. 14–15).
  - There is a heading "Pior caso: probabilidades iguais" (worst case: equal probabilities) at the top of p. 14. The notes do not develop it.
- **Higher-order Huffman (p. 15).**
  - Encode sequences of m symbols. A⁽ᵐ⁾ is the set of those sequences, with size (number of symbols)ᵐ.
  - Example: P(a₁) = 0.8 and P(a₂) = 0.2.
  - (a) First order: the tree uses only a₁ (0.8) and a₂ (0.2), so L = 1 bit/symbol. The final bit assignment (a₁→0 and a₂→1, or the reverse) is hard to read.
- **Second order (p. 16).**
  - The source is memoryless, so P(aᵢaⱼ) = P(aᵢ)P(aⱼ).
  - The four sequences have probabilities a₁a₁ = 0.64, a₁a₂ = 0.16, a₂a₁ = 0.16 and a₂a₂ = 0.04.
  - The tree merges 0.04 and 0.16 into 0.20, then 0.16 and 0.20 into 0.36, then 0.36 against 0.64.
  - L⁽²⁾ is **left unfinished** in the notes. My computation, not in the notes: with lengths 1, 2, 3, 3, L⁽²⁾ = 1.56 bits per pair = 0.78 bit/symbol. The entropy is ≈ 0.722, so the second-order code is better than the first-order 1 bit/symbol.
- **Calculator tip (p. 16).**
  - A calculator computes −x·log x − y·log y in base 10. Convert to base 2 with H = Z / log(2).
- **Summary list at the bottom of p. 16.**
  - Repetition code (channel code, error correction).
  - Information theory: I(A) and H(X).
  - Compression (source coding).
  - Channel coding (detection and correction), starting with the Hamming code. The note says it is "no longer point to point, but vector".

## 5. Hamming code, start (p. 17)
- **Channel model.** Codeword c = [1010011], noise n = [0010000], received r = c + n = [1000011]. The error is in the 3rd bit.
  - Addition is mod 2: 1+0 = 1, 1+1 = 0, 0+0 = 0.
- **Hamming distance d_H(x,y).** The number of differing positions. For x = [1010] and y = [1000], d_H = 1.
- **Encoding example.** The message is m = [0110]. It is multiplied by a generator matrix G with rows:
  - 1101000
  - 0110100
  - 0011010
  - 0001101
- **Tip from the notes.** Because m has 1s in positions 2 and 3, add only rows 2 and 3 of G. So 0110100 + 0011010 = 0101110, which gives c = [0101110]. Then r = c + n.
- The page is unfinished and has no decoding step.
